intro: The most a landlord or letting agent can take as a deposit in England, what must be told to the tenant after paying it, and what a court can order if it is unprotected.
explanation:
## Only a short list of payments can be charged to tenants

The Tenant Fees Act bans most letting fees in England's private rented sector, and it covers tenancy agreements signed or renewed after the ban took effect. A landlord or letting agent can charge rent, a refundable tenancy deposit and a refundable holding deposit. A few other charges are allowed. These include a payment the tenant triggers by asking to end the tenancy early, a default fee for late rent or a lost key where the tenancy agreement provides for one, and a capped charge for changing the tenancy. Tenants can also be charged for what they use, such as utilities, communication services, the TV licence and Council Tax.

The cap on the tenancy deposit depends on annual rent. Rent below {fact:td_high_rent_threshold} a year allows {fact:td_cap_weeks_standard}, and rent at or above that level allows {fact:td_cap_weeks_high_rent}. A holding deposit, which reserves a property before the tenancy begins, is a separate payment with its own limit of {fact:td_holding_deposit_cap}.

This page covers England. The deposit cap described here comes from the Tenant Fees Act, and Scotland and Northern Ireland run their own deposit protection schemes.

## The landlord must protect the deposit and pass on specific details

Within {fact:td_protection_deadline_days} of receiving the deposit, the landlord or letting agent must put it in a government-backed tenancy deposit protection (TDP) scheme. In a custodial scheme, the scheme holds the money for free. In an insured scheme, the landlord or agent keeps it and pays the scheme to insure it. The duty applies even when someone else paid the deposit, such as a parent or a rent deposit scheme.

The tenants must be told the property address, the amount paid and how the deposit is protected. That includes the name and contact details of the scheme and of its dispute resolution service. The landlord or letting agency must also give their own name and contact details, plus those of anyone else who paid the deposit.

Tenants must also be told why some or all of the deposit could be kept, for example to fix damage. They need to know how to claim it back at the end of the tenancy, what to do if they cannot reach the landlord, and what to do if they disagree about the amount returned.

## Tenants can go to court if the deposit was not protected

If a landlord did not use a TDP scheme when required to, the tenants can apply to a county court at any point while the tenancy runs.

If the court finds the deposit was unprotected, it can order the landlord to repay it to the tenants or to pay it into a custodial scheme's bank account. The order carries a fixed deadline for the payment into the account.

The court can also order the landlord to pay the tenants up to {fact:td_penalty_multiple}, within a fixed deadline of the order. It may also decide that the tenants do not have to leave the property when the tenancy ends.
